claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is governed by engineered nanoscale interfaces.
Engineered nanoscale interfaces impede dislocation motion relative to homogeneous coatings.
The as-deposited multilayer coatings contain distinct chemically heterogeneous interfaces.
The as-deposited multilayer coatings contain distinct structurally heterogeneous interfaces.
The proposed homogeneous baseline coatings are single-phase and have the same overall composition as the multilayer coatings.
The controlled comparison holds overall composition and processing conditions constant while changing multilayer architecture.
Diffusion-assisted deformation is active under the proposed elevated-temperature, constant-stress test conditions.
Chemical disorder and lattice mismatch at engineered multilayer interfaces create local stress fields.
Heterogeneous interfaces act as barriers that pin or redirect dislocations.
Interfacial pinning or redirection of dislocations delays the accumulation of creep strain.
Multilayer coatings will exhibit lower creep strain rates than homogeneous coatings under identical test conditions.
Multilayer coatings will exhibit a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to homogeneous coatings.
The proposed mechanism applies when layer thickness remains in the nanoscale range.
The proposed mechanism applies only while extensive diffusion or other interfacial degradation does not destroy interfacial integrity.
Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in creep strain or a delayed onset of plastic deformation in the multilayer coatings would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe dislocation pinning at multilayer interfaces would falsify the proposed interfacial mechanism.
